q: A series loop contains a 20 V source, a 4.0 Ω resistor, a 5.0 Ω resistor, and a second battery V₂ opposing the first source. A meter shows the loop current is 1.0 A. Applying KVL, find V₂, in volts.
explain: KVL around the loop (20 V source taken as positive rise): 20 − (1.0)(4.0) − (1.0)(5.0) − V₂ = 0 → 20 − 4 − 5 = V₂ → V₂ = 11 V. The opposing battery 'uses up' the remaining voltage not dropped across the resistors.

q: The volt is the SI unit of electric potential difference, named after Alessandro Volta. Which ratio correctly expresses one volt?
explain: By definition, 1 V = 1 J/C — one joule of work done moving one coulomb of charge through the potential difference. 1 J/A = V·s (not V); 1 C/J = 1/V; 1 A/Ω = A·(A/V) = A²/V ≠ V (since Ω = V/A, so A/Ω = A²/V).

q: The schematic shows a 12 V battery driving two resistors. Find the voltage across R2.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 150" role="img" aria-label="Series circuit: 12 V battery with a 40 ohm and an 80 ohm resistor"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M30 110 V40 H110 M150 40 H190 M230 40 H290 V110 H30"/><path d="M110 28 h40 v24 h-40 z"/><path d="M190 28 h40 v24 h-40 z"/><path d="M24 100 h12 M20 92 h20 M24 84 h12 M20 76 h20"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle"><text x="130" y="22">R1 = 40 Ω</text><text x="210" y="22">R2 = 80 Ω</text><text x="64" y="90">12 V</text><text x="160" y="135">series loop</text></g></svg>
caption: Two resistors in series across a 12 V source.
explain: In series the same current flows through both: I = V/(R1+R2) = 12/(40+80) = 0.1 A. Then V2 = I x R2 = 0.1 x 80 = 8 V. (Check: V1 = 0.1 x 40 = 4 V, and 4 + 8 = 12 V.)

q: Two identical positive point charges are moved from 1.0 m apart to 0.25 m apart. By what factor does the electric potential energy of the system change?
choices: It increases by a factor of 16
It increases by a factor of 4
It decreases to one-quarter of its original value
explain: Electric potential energy between two point charges: U = kq²/r. Since U is proportional to 1/r, the ratio is U_final/U_initial = r_initial/r_final = 1.0/0.25 = 4. The energy increases by a factor of 4 because the distance decreased by a factor of 4, and work is done against the repulsive force. 'Factor of 16' is the force ratio (F ∝ 1/r²), not the energy ratio. 'Decreases' is wrong because like charges repel — bringing them closer always raises the potential energy.

q: A 120 Ω resistor is connected directly across a sinusoidal AC source whose peak voltage is 170 V. What is the average power, in watts, dissipated by the resistor?
explain: Average power in a resistive AC load requires RMS values, not peak values. Step 1 — find V_rms: V_rms = V_peak / √2 = 170 / 1.4142 ≈ 120.2 V. Step 2 — compute power: P = V_rms² / R = (170)² / (2 × 120) = 28900 / 240 ≈ 120 W. A common error is using V_peak directly, giving P = 170²/120 ≈ 241 W — exactly twice the correct answer, because P_avg = P_peak / 2 for a sine wave.

q: A copper wire has a resistance of 6.0 Ω. The wire is then drawn through a die until its length exactly doubles; its volume and resistivity remain unchanged throughout. What is the resistance of the stretched wire, in ohms?
explain: Resistance R = ρL/A. Because volume V = L·A is constant, doubling the length (L′ = 2L) forces the cross-sectional area to halve (A′ = A/2). New resistance: R′ = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4·(ρL/A) = 4R₀ = 4 × 6.0 = 24 Ω. A common error is concluding R only doubles because L doubled — that ignores the simultaneous halving of A that constant volume requires.

q: A GFCI outlet trips when it senses a difference greater than about 5 mA between the current in the hot conductor and the current in the neutral conductor. In which scenario would the GFCI NOT protect the person involved?
choices: A person standing on wet concrete touches the metal case of a defective power tool and current flows through their body to ground
A person simultaneously grasps the hot prong and the neutral prong of an unplugged extension cord, forming a hand-to-hand current path
A hair dryer falls into a water-filled sink, sending current from the hot wire through the water to the grounded metal drain
Damaged cord insulation allows the hot conductor to contact the grounded metal frame of an appliance
explain: The GFCI measures |I_hot − I_neutral|. In choice B current leaves through the hot prong, travels hand-to-hand through the person, and returns through the neutral prong. Both conductors carry identical current, so the difference is zero and the GFCI never trips — the person receives a shock with no protection. Choices A, C, and D all route current to ground without it returning through neutral, creating an imbalance that trips the GFCI within milliseconds.
